los.html:
1Introduction, consent, position at 45°, expose the chest.
2. General inspectionBreathlessness, cyanosis, pallor, scars (sternotomy, thoracotomy, saphenous vein harvest), pacemaker, around the bed (GTN spray, oxygen).
3. HandsClubbing, splinter haemorrhages, Janeway lesions, Osler's nodes (endocarditis), xanthomata, capillary refill, temperature.
4. PulseRadial rate and rhythm, radio-radial delay, collapsing pulse (aortic regurgitation); blood pressure.
5. FaceConjunctival pallor, xanthelasma, malar flush (mitral stenosis), central cyanosis.
6. NeckJVP (height, waveform; hepatojugular reflux), carotid pulse (character: slow-rising in aortic stenosis).
7Chest inspection, then apex beat (normally 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line; displaced in LV dilatation), heaves and thrills.
8. Auscultation
  • Aortic (right 2nd ICS), pulmonary (left 2nd ICS), tricuspid (left lower sternal edge), mitral (apex)
  • Time with the carotid pulse.
  • Manoeuvres: left lateral position, bell at the apex (mitral stenosis)
  • Sitting forward, held expiration (aortic regurgitation)
  • Listen over the carotids (radiation of aortic stenosis) and axilla (mitral regurgitation).
9Lung bases (crackles), sacral and ankle oedema.
10. FinishPeripheral pulses, ECG, urine dip (endocarditis), fundoscopy.

los.text: Identify red flag symptoms and signs in a cardiovascular history that require urgent attention
los.html:
SymptomRed flag / urgent cause
Chest pain at rest, crushing, radiating to arm/jaw, with sweatingAcute coronary syndrome
Sudden tearing pain radiating to the backAortic dissection
Syncope on exertionAortic stenosis, HOCM, arrhythmia
Syncope with palpitations or no warning, family history of sudden deathArrhythmia (long QT, Brugada)
Breathlessness at rest, orthopnoea, PND, frothy sputumAcute heart failure
Pleuritic pain with breathlessness, leg swellingPulmonary embolism
Sudden cold, painful, pale legAcute limb ischaemia
  • Signs: hypotension, new murmur, irregular pulse, raised JVP, low sats.

los.text: Explain the purpose of signposting in clinical communication and demonstrate its use during consultation
los.html:
SignpostingTelling the patient what is coming next, so the consultation feels organised and they can follow it.
Examples
  • "I'm now going to ask some questions about your general health", "I'd like to explain what we think is happening, then talk about the next steps.
  • Is that OK?"
Benefit
Patient knows what to expect
Smooth transitions between sections
Gives the patient a chance to add things
Helps the patient remember information (chunking)

los.text: Describe the basic components of an ECG and interpret common abnormalities
los.html:
• Leads: 12 views from 10 electrodes: limb leads (I, II, III, aVR, aVL, aVF) and chest leads (V1–V6).
ComponentRepresentsNormal
P waveAtrial depolarisationBefore every QRS
PR intervalAV conduction0.12–0.20 s (3–5 small squares)
QRS complexVentricular depolarisation<0.12 s (3 small squares)
ST segmentEarly repolarisationIsoelectric
T waveVentricular repolarisationUpright in most leads
QT intervalDepolarisation to repolarisationQTc <450 ms (men), <470 ms (women)
  • Rate: 300 ÷ number of large squares between R waves (regular), or QRS count in 10 s × 6.
AbnormalityFeatures
Atrial fibrillationIrregularly irregular, no P waves
STEMIST elevation in contiguous leads (e.g. II, III, aVF inferior; V1–V4 anterior)
First-degree heart blockPR >0.2 s
Complete heart blockP waves and QRS independent
LBBB / RBBBBroad QRS; "WiLLiaM" / "MaRRoW" patterns
HyperkalaemiaTall tented T waves, broad QRS
